text: And then, in a letter home that would send chills down your spine, the young prospector wrote the words that would haunt his family forever. Words that revealed everything. “I fear I shall not see the spring.”
strengths: the quotation itself is plain and moving
weaknesses: a fake dramatic beat to open
tells the listener to shiver before they have heard a word of the letter
two sentences of fanfare for a single line
spokenRhythm: A long portentous sentence, a fragment of build-up, then the quotation, which has to compete with its own introduction.
narrativeFunction: Meant to deliver a prospector's letter home, but spends its words announcing how important the letter is.
whyItFails: The set-up tells the listener how to react, that the words are chilling and haunting and reveal everything, so the quotation can only disappoint. And then is a fake dramatic beat, and forever is trailer language. The prospector's own sentence is strong enough to stand after a plain introduction.
rewrite: In a letter home, the young prospector wrote, “I fear I shall not see the spring.”

text: The mine manager's report said, “The lower levels cannot be worked without pumps, and the company has no money for pumps.” The problem? Money. It wasn't an engineering problem, in other words, but a financial one.
strengths: the manager's sentence is clear and says everything needed
weaknesses: explains a quotation the listener has just understood
a question answered by a one-word fragment
a contrast formula restating the quotation a third time
spokenRhythm: A clean quotation, then a question with a one-word answer, then a long sentence repeating what the quotation said.
narrativeFunction: Meant to explain why the mine could go no deeper, but says it three times.
whyItFails: The manager's own words already make the point, and plainly. Everything after the quotation restates it, first as a quiz and then as a not X but Y formula, which treats the audience as if they hadn't been listening. Narration around a quotation should set it up and then get out of its way.
rewrite: The mine manager's report said, “The lower levels cannot be worked without pumps, and the company has no money for pumps.”

text: “Gentlemen,” the chairman might have said, leaning forward over the polished table, his voice barely a whisper, “we are finished.” You can almost feel the silence that followed. The bank closed its doors the next morning.
strengths: the closing fact is plain and strong
weaknesses: invents a quotation and excuses it with might have
describes a posture and a voice that no source records
tells the listener what the silence felt like
spokenRhythm: An invented line of dialogue broken up by stage business, a sentence of mood, then the only fact.
narrativeFunction: Meant to dramatise the night before the bank failed, but replaces the record with a scene from a play.
whyItFails: Might have said does not make an invented quotation honest. The listener hears words in quotation marks and remembers them as spoken, and if the chairman were a real person the film would be putting words in his mouth. The leaning and the whisper are stage directions, and the silence is the narrator's feeling, not the record's.
rewrite: We can't know what the chairman said. The bank closed its doors the next morning.

text: “The machine is perfectly safe in any wind,” its designer told the newspapers. But was it? Could anyone really promise that about a machine made of spruce and linen? Its first passengers believed him, and they shouldn't have.
strengths: the designer's claim is a clean, quotable line
spruce and linen is a concrete detail
weaknesses: two rhetorical questions in a row after the quotation
the questions do the listener's doubting for them
ends on a hint of disaster instead of what happened
spokenRhythm: A quotation, two questions in a row, and a closing line that hints at disaster without naming it.
narrativeFunction: Meant to cast doubt on a designer's promise, but does it by quizzing the listener.
whyItFails: The questions doubt the claim on the audience's behalf, when the audience would doubt it anyway once they heard what the machine was made of. Two in a row is a habit of generated narration. The last clause withholds what went wrong in order to sound ominous, when a plain statement would be stronger.
rewrite: Its designer told the newspapers, “The machine is perfectly safe in any wind.” It was made of spruce and linen. Its first passengers believed him, and he was wrong.

text: Her hands trembling, the relief officer dipped her pen — and wrote the words that would define the famine. “The meal is gone.” Here's the thing — she wrote them in October, before the winter had even begun.
strengths: the October date is a strong, specific fact
weaknesses: trembling hands and a dipped pen are invented gestures
here's the thing announces the one fact that matters
words that would define the famine is trailer language
spokenRhythm: A breathless sentence broken by a dash, a short quotation, then a second dash before the fact.
narrativeFunction: Meant to give the relief officer's report and its timing, but performs the moment instead of reporting it.
whyItFails: Nobody recorded her hands, and if the picture shows the letter, the gesture is the camera's job anyway. Here's the thing is a presenter's tic that makes the October date sound like a trick. The date is alarming on its own when it is said plainly after the quotation.
rewrite: The relief officer wrote, “The meal is gone.” She wrote it in October, before the winter had begun.
